lesson.title: Natural Selection: How Differential Survival Shapes Populations
lesson.summary: Natural selection is the process by which heritable traits that improve survival and reproduction in a given environment become more common in a population over successive generations.
lesson.body:
Natural selection requires three ingredients, each one established in the chapters leading up to this point. First, heritable variation must exist within a population, individuals must genuinely differ from one another in ways that trace back to genotype, exactly the kind of variation covered in the chapter on variation in populations. Second, that variation must actually be heritable, capable of being passed from parent to offspring, which is why heritability matters so much, only heritable variation can accumulate across generations. Third, individuals must differ in survival and reproductive success because of that variation, with the environment favoring some variants over others.

It helps to be precise about the mechanism, because natural selection does not act with foresight or intention. Organisms are not trying to adapt, and no outside force is choosing which traits are best. It is simply a statistical consequence of the three ingredients above. Individuals whose heritable traits happen to make them better suited to their current environment tend, on average, to survive longer and produce more offspring than individuals without those traits. Over many generations, those advantageous traits become more common in the population. This was Darwin's central insight, combined directly with Malthus's observation, discussed in the chapter on Darwin's observations, that more offspring are produced in every generation than available resources can support, creating an ongoing struggle for existence that gives selection something to act on.

The finches Darwin collected in the Galapagos provide a concrete and well documented illustration, extended by decades of direct observation. On the island of Daphne Major, biologists Peter and Rosemary Grant have studied a population of medium ground finches for many years. During a severe drought, the small, soft seeds the finches normally preferred became scarce, leaving mainly large, tough seeds as the remaining food supply. Birds with larger, deeper beaks were better able to crack these tough seeds and survive the drought, while many smaller beaked birds died. Because beak size is heritable, the birds that survived passed their larger beak trait on to their offspring, and the average beak size in the population measurably increased in the very next generation. That single case shows all three ingredients of natural selection, heritable variation, differential survival, and an environment favoring certain traits, operating together within one population over just a few years.

One more point is worth being explicit about. Natural selection acts on populations, not on individuals. An individual does not evolve during its own lifetime, its genotype does not change in response to selection pressure. What changes, generation after generation, is the frequency of different traits across the population as a whole. Biologists often summarize how strongly selection favors one genotype over another using a single measure, relative fitness, the subject of the next chapter.
